messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 47
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Bus Driver
- Trauma Type: Police
- Pcl5: 48

He is 47, a bus driver who has spent most of his adult life moving other people safely from one stop to the next. Before the event, he likes the predictability of the work: the early checks of mirrors and brakes, the rhythm of traffic lights, the familiar faces climbing aboard with coffee cups and grocery bags. He lives alone, keeps mostly to himself, and takes some pride in being the kind of driver who stays calm when riders are agitated or the roads are bad. He says he has always believed that if he follows the rules and treats people with respect, things usually work out.

That belief is badly shaken one evening after his shift, when he is pulled over by police a few blocks from home. He remembers the flashing lights filling the inside of the bus with blue and red, turning the empty seats into something unreal. He assumes there has been some misunderstanding and reaches for his wallet when an officer begins shouting. The pace of the encounter changes so quickly that he still struggles to put it into words. He is ordered off the bus, pushed against the side of it, and handcuffed. He can feel the metal cutting into his wrists and the rough paint of the bus against his cheek. He keeps trying to explain who he is, where he works, that he has just finished his route. The more he speaks, the more the officers seem to read him as noncompliant. He remembers one hand pressing between his shoulder blades, another officer searching him, the humiliation of passing cars slowing down to watch. What stays with him most is the helplessness: the sudden understanding that he is no longer being seen as a person with a job and a routine and a name, but as a threat.

He is released later, after the error becomes clear, but by then something in him has changed. In the days afterward he tells himself to move on. He returns to work because that is what he has always done. Yet when he sees a patrol car in his rearview mirror, his chest tightens so sharply that he loses his breath. He starts gripping the steering wheel hard enough that his hands cramp. At red lights he checks his mirrors over and over, scanning for flashing lights. If a police cruiser pulls up beside the bus, he feels heat rush through his body and his thoughts narrow to one desperate wish: don’t look at me.

At night he replays the stop in fragments. He sees the reflected lights on the windshield, hears the officer’s voice rising, feels again the pressure of being pinned against the bus. Sleep becomes thin and broken. Sometimes he jolts awake already sweating, convinced for a moment that someone is standing over him. He begins leaving the television on because silence makes room for the memory. In the morning he is exhausted and irritable, embarrassed by how brittle he has become.

Over the next several months, he starts reorganizing his life around avoidance. He changes his route home to steer clear of the street where he was stopped. He skips gas stations where police cars sometimes idle. On his days off he stays inside his apartment with the blinds half closed. Friends from work ask him to join them for coffee after a shift, but he usually declines, saying he is tired. He does not tell them that crowded places make him feel exposed, or that he constantly scans doorways and windows without meaning to. He has begun to experience the city as if danger can appear anywhere, without warning, and ordinary errands now require a kind of mental rehearsal.

The hardest part for him is what happens on the job. Driving used to calm him. Now he feels on edge before he even starts the engine. He notices every siren, every abrupt movement on the sidewalk, every car that follows too long behind the bus. When passengers argue or raise their voices, his body reacts before his mind catches up; his heart pounds and his shoulders tense as if he is bracing for impact. He has become more curt with riders, then ashamed afterward. A few times he pulls the bus over because he feels dizzy and cannot focus. He worries constantly that his fear will show, that passengers will see his hands shaking as he reaches for the radio.

Being alone gives him too much time to think, but being around people is tiring in a different way. He says he feels “smaller” than he used to, less sure of himself. He no longer assumes that authority means safety. He watches officers on platforms and street corners and feels anger, fear, and confusion all at once. Part of him wants to confront what happened; another part wants never to be noticed again.

By the time he speaks about it in a fuller way, he describes living as if his body has not understood that the incident is over. He knows, logically, that not every police car means danger. He knows he is back at work, back in his apartment, back in the routines that once defined him. But his mind keeps returning to that evening beside the bus, and his body keeps preparing for it to happen again.
